In Korean the particle or ending next to 사람 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. 연기.nuance: 연기 is the noun; 연기하다 is the verb 'to act/perform.'
연기.explanation: 연기 (yeongi) = "acting / performance". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 연기가 자연스러운 것 같아요. ("I think the acting seems natural.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 연기, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
연기.shortExplanation: 연기 means "acting / performance" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

usagePhrases.en: I think the acting seems natural.
usagePhrases.note: 자연스럽다 is ㅂ-irregular: 자연스러운.

examples.en: The actors' performances were really good, you know.

ex.ko: 물가 상승이 가계에 경제적 부담을 주고 있다.
ex.en: Rising prices are placing an economic burden on households.
ex.note: 경제적 with no 인 — the compressed modifier form of written Korean.

경제.nuance: 경제 (經濟, 經 'manage/govern' + 濟 'aid/relieve' — from 經世濟民 'govern the world and relieve the people') means 'the economy' as a system. The biggest learner trap is the adjective 경제적이다, which splits into TWO everyday meanings: (1) 'economical', i.e. money-saving (버스가 더 경제적이에요), and (2) 'economic/financial' (경제적 부담 = financial burden) — context decides which. Equally important is the slump idiom: to say the economy is doing badly, Korean uses 경제가 어렵다 or 경제가 안 좋다, NOT a literal 경제가 나쁘다, because 어렵다 ('hard, strained') is the conventional collocation. Keep 경제 (the system/field) distinct from 경영 (經營, business management of a company); they look similar but 경영 is running a firm.
경제.explanation: 경제 (gyeongje) = "economy". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 경제가 어렵다 ("the economy is bad / struggling") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 경제, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
경제.shortExplanation: 경제 means "economy" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Translating 'the economy is bad' word-for-word as 경제가 나쁘다. Natural Korean is 경제가 어렵다 or 경제가 안 좋다.
Forgetting that 경제적이다 can mean 'economical (saves money)', so '이게 더 경제적이에요' means 'this is cheaper/more cost-effective', not 'this is more economic'.

usagePhrases.note: 어렵다 (lit. 'difficult') is the idiomatic way to say the economy is in a slump, not 나쁘다.
Standard compound (성장 = growth); 경제 성장률 = the economic growth rate.
Two senses: 'economical (cheap)' and 'economic/financial' (경제적 부담 = financial burden).
경제 takes scope modifiers directly: 세계 경제, 한국 경제, 지역 경제.

examples.en: The economy is tough these days.
examples.note: Plain version of the key idiom: 경제가 어렵다 = 'the economy is struggling', using 어렵다 not 나쁘다.

examples.ko: 정부는 경제 성장을 위해 여러 정책을 내놓았어요.
examples.romanization: jeongbuneun gyeongje seongjangeul wihae yeoreo jeongchaegeul naenoasseoyo.
examples.en: The government put forward various policies for economic growth.
examples.note: 경제 성장을 위해 = 'for economic growth'; 내놓다 = 'put forward (a plan/policy)'.

examples.en: Using public transportation is much more economical.
examples.note: Here 경제적이다 = 'economical / cost-saving' — the everyday wallet-friendly sense, not 'economic'.

ex.ko: 이 정도 문제는 그 사람 실력이면 식은 죽 먹기예요.
ex.en: With his ability, a problem at this level is a piece of cake.
ex.note: 식은 죽 먹기 acts as a noun and simply takes 예요.

실력.nuance: 실력 is not confidence or effort; it is the ability itself.
실력.explanation: "skill level / actual ability" is 실력 (sillyeok). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 연습할수록 실력이 늘어요. ("The more you practice, the more your skill improves."). Watch the particle attached to 실력 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
실력.shortExplanation: 실력 means "skill level / actual ability" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Say 실력이 늘어요 for ability improving, not 실력이 커요.

usagePhrases.en: The more you practice, the more your skill improves.
usagePhrases.note: A clean proportional sentence for -(으)ㄹ수록.

examples.en: The more you use Korean, the more your ability improves.
examples.note: 실력이 늘다 is the natural collocation.

ex.ko: 원자재 가격이 오르면서 제품 가격도 인상될 전망이다.
ex.en: As raw material prices rise, product prices are also expected to be raised.
ex.note: 인상되다 is the formal passive of 인상하다; news avoids the plain 오르다 for deliberate rises.

가격.nuance: 가격(價格) is Sino-Korean — 價 'value/price' + 格 'standard' — so it literally means the 'value-standard' set on a thing, the official posted price. Its native-Korean twin is 값, and the line is feel and register: 값 is shorter, warmer, and used in fixed everyday phrases (값이 싸다, 값을 치르다), while 가격 sounds more neutral and 'tag/system' (가격표 price tag, 가격 인상 price hike) and is what you read on signs. The biggest English-speaker trap is the adjective: a high price is 비싸요 (expensive), a low price is 싸요 (cheap) — Koreans do NOT say 가격이 높아요/낮아요 the way English says 'high/low price', so importing 'high' here sounds off. Note too that to ask a clerk you rarely say the noun at all: the natural line is just 얼마예요? ('how much?'). 가격 collocates with 비싸다, 싸다, 오르다 (rise), 내리다 (drop), and 깎다 (haggle down).
가격.explanation: 가격 (gagyeok) means "price". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 가격이 비싸요 ("the price is high"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 가격 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.
가격.shortExplanation: 가격 means "price" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 가격이 높아요 for 'the price is high' — that is a direct translation of English; Korean uses 비싸요 (expensive). Use 높다/낮다 only for height or numbers like temperature, not for prices.
Treating 가격 and 값 as freely swappable — they overlap, but you say 값을 치르다 (pay the price), not 가격을 치르다, and 가격표 (price tag), not 값표. Learn them as set phrases.
Asking a shopkeeper 가격이 뭐예요? ('what is the price?'). The natural question is 얼마예요? or 가격이 얼마예요?, never 뭐예요 for an amount.

usagePhrases.note: with prices Korean says 비싸다/싸다 (expensive/cheap), never 높다/낮다
object marker 을 + 물어보다 'ask and see'
깎다 'to shave/cut' is the verb for haggling
drop the particle in speech; 좀 softens the request

examples.ko: 가격은 좀 비싼데 품질이 좋아서 살게요.

examples.en: The price is a bit high, but the quality is good so I'll buy it.

ex.ko: 회의는 이미 끝났으며 결과는 곧 공유될 예정임.
ex.en: The meeting has already ended, and the outcome will be shared shortly.
ex.note: -(으)며 plus a -(으)ㅁ close: two written layers in one short line.

회의.nuance: 회의 (漢字 會議, 會 'gather' + 議 'discuss') is a formal, work-style meeting where people gather to discuss and decide something — a board meeting, a team sync, a planning session. The near-synonym learners reach for is 모임, but 모임 is a social get-together (a dinner, a club, friends meeting up) with no agenda, so calling drinks with friends a 회의 sounds robotic; conversely calling a budget review a 모임 sounds too loose. It pairs naturally with 회의를 하다 (hold), 회의에 들어가다 (go into), 회의가 길어지다 (run long). The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: you are *in* a meeting as a location, so the action takes 회의에서, but you *enter* a meeting with 회의에 들어가다 — and never confuse 회의 with the look-alike 회사 (company) or 회비 (membership fee).
회의.explanation: 회의 (hoeui) means "meeting". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 회의가 있어요. ("There is a meeting."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 회의 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.
회의.shortExplanation: 회의 means "meeting" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 친구하고 회의했어요 for hanging out with friends — 회의 implies a formal agenda; for a casual gathering say 친구하고 모였어요 or use 모임.
Using 회의에 for where talking happens, as in 회의에 이야기했어요 — the location of an action needs 에서: 회의에서 이야기했어요. Reserve 회의에 for 들어가다/참석하다.
Mixing up 회의 with 회사; 회사에 가요 means go to the company/office, while 회의에 가요 means go to the meeting.

usagePhrases.note: Existence with 있다 plus subject 이/가 — the default way to announce a meeting on the calendar.
회의에 들어가다 'enter a meeting' is the set phrase; use 에 here, not 에서, because you are moving in.
회의 takes 하다 to become a verb; 회의하다 = the act of meeting, distinct from the event noun.
Bare noun + 시간 forms a time phrase; no particle between 회의 and 시간.

examples.en: I have two meetings today.
examples.note: Counts meetings with 개; 회의가 (subject) is what 있다 describes.

examples.en: We decided a new plan in the meeting.
examples.note: 에서 marks the meeting as the place where the action happened — contrast with 에 for entering.

examples.ko: 부장님이 회의를 길게 끌어서 다들 지쳤어요.
examples.romanization: bujangnimi hoeuireul gilge kkeureoseo dadeul jichyeosseoyo.
examples.en: The manager dragged the meeting out, so everyone got worn out.
examples.note: Real-office register: 회의를 끌다 'drag a meeting out' is the natural complaint collocation.

ex.ko: 새 정책은 다음 주 월요일에 발표될 것으로 알려졌다.
ex.en: The new policy is understood to be announced next Monday.
ex.note: -(으)ㄹ 것으로 알려졌다: reported, but not confirmed by the paper.

발표.nuance: 발표(發表)는 '필 발 + 겉 표', 곧 '안에 있던 것을 겉으로 드러내 알림'이라는 뜻으로, 여러 사람 앞에서 자기 생각이나 조사한 내용을 말로 알리는 것을 가리켜요. 비슷한 '연설'은 정치인·대표가 청중에게 행하는 더 공식적이고 일방적인 말하기라 학교 과제에는 안 어울리고, '공지'는 '날짜·결과를 알리는 통보'라 말로 설명하는 발표와 다르며, '보고'는 윗사람에게 결과를 전달하는 데 초점이 있어요. 그래서 학생이 수업에서 하는 것은 '발표'가 딱 맞아요. '발표하다' 동사와 '발표를 하다' 형태가 둘 다 자연스럽고, '발표 준비/자료/순서'와 잘 어울려요. 한 가지 더, '합격자 발표'처럼 결과를 공표한다는 뜻도 있어 영어 announce와 겹치지만, 수업 맥락에서는 말로 설명하는 presentation을 뜻한다는 점을 구분하세요.
발표.explanation: 발표 (balpyo) = "presentation, announcing (in class)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 발표를 하다 ("give a presentation") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 발표, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.
발표.shortExplanation: 발표 means "presentation, announcing (in class)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
'발표를 말하다'는 같은 뜻을 두 번 말한 겹말이라 어색해요. '발표를 하다' 또는 '발표하다'면 충분합니다.
'발표' 자체가 동사 '발표하다'로 쓰이니 'I will presentation'처럼 영어식으로 '발표할 거예요'를 빼먹고 명사만 던지면 문장이 안 돼요. 동사형을 꼭 붙이세요.
결과를 알리는 '합격자 발표'와 수업의 '구두 발표'를 같은 말로 뭉뚱그리지 마세요. 맥락에 따라 announce인지 oral presentation인지 구분해야 의미가 분명합니다.

usagePhrases.note: 붙여서 '발표하다' 한 단어로도 자연스러워요
발표 + 준비로 미리 갖추는 일을 가리켜요
긴장은 '떨리다', 주어는 '발표가'예요
'자료'는 슬라이드·유인물 같은 받침 자료예요

examples.en: I'm giving a presentation in class tomorrow.
examples.note: 때를 나타내는 '수업 시간에'처럼 시점에는 '-에'를 붙여요.

examples.en: I finished preparing my presentation yesterday.
examples.note: '다'는 '남김없이/모두'라는 뜻의 부사예요.

examples.en: I'm so nervous about presenting in front of people.
examples.note: '-(으)려니까'는 '~하려고 하니까'로 의도와 그에 따른 심정을 이어요.

ex.ko: 자료를 검토하고자 담당자에게 원본을 요청했다.
ex.en: I requested the originals from the person in charge in order to review the materials.
ex.note: -고자 states the purpose, with one subject across both clauses.

자료.nuance: 자료 can mean data, but in daily work and study talk it often means the file, handout, or slide deck someone needs.
자료.explanation: 자료 (jaryo) means "materials; data; documents". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 자료를 보내다 ("to send the materials"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 자료 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.
자료.shortExplanation: 자료 means "materials; data; documents" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 정보 for every kind of material. 정보 is information; 자료 is often the actual file or reference material.
Confusing 자료 with 의견. 의견 means opinion.

usagePhrases.note: Common team or class message.
Slides or handouts for a presentation.

examples.en: I will send the materials before the meeting.
examples.note: Practical work or study-group sentence.

ex.ko: 접수는 오늘 오후 여섯 시에 마감되므로 서둘러 주시기 바랍니다.
ex.en: Intake closes at six this afternoon, so please hurry.
ex.note: -(으)므로 can be followed by a request, which -아서/어서 could not.

마감.nuance: 마감 is a native Korean noun (from the verb 막다 'to block/close off') meaning the point at which something is sealed shut: a report's due date, an application cutoff, a shop's last order, even a magazine going to press. The near-synonym confusion is with 기한 and 데드라인: 기한 (期限) is the dry, official 'time limit/term' you see on documents (제출 기한), while 마감 feels more like the live moment things close, and 데드라인 is a borrowed buzzword. Its signature collocation is the idiom 마감에 쫓기다 (chased by the deadline), the universal way to describe last-minute panic. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 'meet a deadline' onto 만나다 ('meet a person'): you do NOT 마감을 만나다 — you 마감을 지키다 (keep/protect it). Note 지키다 is the same verb used for keeping a promise (약속을 지키다), which is the right mental image.
마감.explanation: "deadline; closing (date)" is 마감 (magam). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 마감이 언제예요? ("when is the deadline?"). Watch the particle attached to 마감 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.
마감.shortExplanation: 마감 means "deadline; closing (date)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 마감을 만나다 from English 'meet the deadline' — 만나다 is only for meeting people; the correct collocation is 마감을 지키다 ('protect/keep')
Defaulting to 데드라인 in formal writing — it sounds like office slang; written/official Korean prefers 마감 or 기한

일정.nuance: 일정 is the planned schedule of where you go and what you do, day by day — for a trip, but equally for work or events. The hanja 日程 is 日 (day) + 程 (journey/measure), an 'apportioning of the days'. Distinguish it from 시간 (time, clock time) and 계획 (plan): 시간 is just the hour on the clock, 계획 is the broad intention ('I plan to save money'), while 일정 is the concrete time-tabled sequence of items. Note the signature verb 짜다 — you 일정을 짜다 (literally 'weave a schedule'), the same verb used for 계획을 짜다. Watch the adjective 빡빡하다 / 바쁘다 for a packed itinerary. English-speaker pitfall: don't reach for 시간 when you mean the agenda — '오늘 시간이 어때요?' asks if someone is free, but '오늘 일정이 어때요?' asks about the day's plan.
일정.explanation: "itinerary" is 일정 (iljeong). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 일정을 짜다 ("to make a schedule"). Watch the particle attached to 일정 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.
일정.shortExplanation: 일정 means "itinerary" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 시간 when you mean the itinerary. 시간 = clock time / availability; 일정 = the planned agenda. '시간 있어요?' means 'are you free?', whereas '일정 어때요?' asks about the schedule.
Pairing 일정 with 만들다. Korean weaves a schedule, so the verb is 짜다 — '일정을 짜다'. '일정을 만들다' (make a schedule) sounds unnatural for trip-planning.

참석하다.nuance: 참석하다 is Sino-Korean 參席 — 參 'take part' + 席 'seat' — literally 'take one's seat (and take part)', i.e. attend a formal event like a meeting, ceremony, or banquet. Its register is more formal than just 가다 'to go'; you 결혼식에 가요 casually but 결혼식에 참석합니다 in polite/written contexts. Distinguish it from its close cousin 참가하다 (參加, 'participate/enter'): 참석하다 emphasizes being PRESENT and seated at a gathering, while 참가하다 emphasizes actively TAKING PART (참가하다 fits a contest, race, or program — 대회에 참가하다). The big English-speaker pitfall is the particle: English 'attend THE meeting' (object) drives learners to 회의를 참석하다, but Korean uses 에 — 회의에 참석하다 — because you 'join INTO' the event. As a noun+하다 verb it conjugates on 하다 (참석해요, 참석했어요, formal 참석합니다); negative/impossible split the noun (참석 안 해요, 참석 못 해요).
참석하다.explanation: "to attend" in Korean is 참석하다 (chamseokada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 참석해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 참석하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 회의에 참석하다 ("to attend a meeting") — then reshape the same stem into 참석하고 싶어요 (desire), 참석할 수 있어요 (ability), and 참석 못 해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
참석하다.shortExplanation: 참석하다 means "to attend" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 참석하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 참석해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 회의를 참석해요 because English makes the meeting an object — Korean marks the event with 에: 회의에 참석해요.
Using 참석하다 for a contest or competition — being present at a gathering is 참석하다, but actively competing/taking part is 참가하다: 대회에 참가하다.
Forming the negative as 안 참석해요 — split it: 참석 안 해요 (impossible = 참석 못 해요).

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 참석하다 becomes 참석할 수 있어요 ("can") and 참석할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

결과.nuance: 결과 (結果, literally '結 form/bear + 果 fruit', i.e. the fruit that an action bears) is the end outcome of an action or event, and it almost always pairs with 나오다 (come out) or 나타나다 (appear) rather than any verb of 'making'. Its built-in partner is 과정 (the process leading up to it) and its mirror image is 원인 (the cause behind it), so Koreans constantly say 과정도 중요하고 결과도 중요하다. Register is neutral — fine in a doctor's office (검사 결과), a classroom (시험 결과), or a news report. The big English-speaker trap is twofold: first, you do not 'get' a result with a transitive verb the way English does — the result 나오다 (comes out) on its own and takes 이/가, so 결과를 나오다 is wrong; second, do not confuse the outcome 결과 with the reason 원인/이유 — 결과 is what happened at the end, never why.
결과.explanation: "result, outcome" is 결과 (gyeolgwa). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 시험 결과 ("exam results"). Watch the particle attached to 결과 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
결과.shortExplanation: 결과 means "result, outcome" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't say 결과를 나오다 — 나오다 ('come out') is intransitive, so the result takes 이/가: 결과가 나오다.
결과 is the outcome, not the cause; for 'the reason/cause' use 원인 (objective cause) or 이유 (personal reason), e.g. 사고의 원인, not 사고의 결과, when you mean what triggered it.
Don't force an English plural — there is no 결과들 in 'exam results'; 시험 결과 already covers singular and plural.

ㅠㅠ.nuance: ㅠㅠ is pure visual: the Korean vowel letter ㅠ is reused as a picture of two eyes with tears streaming down (its twin ㅜㅜ is the same face with eyes scrunched), so it's read with the EYES, not pronounced — there's no spoken 'yuyu.' It's one of the most common feeling-markers in Korean chat, and crucially its range runs from genuine sadness all the way to playful, exaggerated 'aw man / waaah' whining; more letters = more drama, often tongue-in-cheek. The English-speaker pitfalls are mostly mechanical and tonal. Mechanically: Koreans attach it with NO space, fused to the last word (취소됐어ㅠㅠ), where English would float an emoji after a space — a gap (휴무래 ㅠㅠ) reads slightly off. Tonally: because it's text and a little cute, English speakers sometimes drop it into semi-professional messages thinking it's neutral like 🙁 — but in a formal or work note it reads as childish and unprofessional, so leave it for friends and dating partners; to a boss, put the feeling in words (아쉽네요/속상하네요) instead. And don't read every ㅠㅠ as real tears; very often it's just light 'ugh, bummer.' Its blends ㅋㅋㅠㅠ / ㅎㅠ even mix laughing-while-crying ('I'm dying').
ㅠㅠ.explanation: "crying emoticon — ㅠㅠ or ㅜㅜ looks like teary eyes. Shows sadness, frustration, or playful whining. (casual slang — friends and peers; not for formal messages)" — that is ㅠㅠ (yuyu (the letters yu-yu; read as a crying-face emoticon, not spoken)). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like ㅠㅠ ("crying / so sad"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.
ㅠㅠ.shortExplanation: ㅠㅠ is a practical expression meaning "crying emoticon — ㅠㅠ or ㅜㅜ looks like teary eyes. Shows sadness, frustration, or playful whining. (casual slang — friends and peers; not for formal messages)".
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.

ㅇㅇ.nuance: ㅇㅇ is the texted form of 응 (eung, casual 'yeah'), doubled to 응응, so it carries pure banmal — the informal register you'd use with people you speak 반말 to out loud. That register IS the meaning: it broadcasts 'we're equals/close.' Its near-neighbor is the polite 네/넵, and the gap between them is exactly the politeness gap, which is why the English-speaker pitfall is severe: English 'yeah' is fine to almost anyone, but firing ㅇㅇ at a boss, professor, or older stranger skips every layer of politeness and reads as blunt, even disrespectful — like grunting 'uh-huh' at a superior. The safe upgrade ladder for seniors is 네 (polite) → 넵 (cheerful-polite) → 네네 (warm). Don't confuse ㅇㅇ (yes/agreement, from 응응) with ㅇㅋ (okay/got it, from 오케이): you ANSWER a yes/no question with ㅇㅇ, but you CONFIRM an instruction with ㅇㅋ. And length carries warmth — a bare ㅇㅇ to a friend who's clearly excited can read as flat, even reluctant, so match their energy with ㅇㅇㅇㅇ or 응응!!; worse, a single curt ㅇ alone can feel like an annoyed 'k.'
ㅇㅇ.explanation: ㅇㅇ (oo (eung-eung)) = "yeah / yep — casual yes, from 응응 (the casual 응 = yeah). A quick agreement. (casual slang — only with friends or close peers, never to a boss or elder)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: ㅇㅇ ("yeah"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.
ㅇㅇ.shortExplanation: ㅇㅇ is a practical expression meaning "yeah / yep — casual yes, from 응응 (the casual 응 = yeah). A quick agreement. (casual slang — only with friends or close peers, never to a boss or elder)".
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Replying ㅇㅇ to a boss, professor, or elder — it's banmal and skips all politeness, sounding blunt and rude; use 네 / 넵 / 네네 instead
Using ㅇㅇ to answer 'okay, got it' on an instruction — that's ㅇㅋ's job (from 오케이); ㅇㅇ is for 'yes' to a yes/no question (from 응응)
Carrying over English 'yeah' as universally casual-but-fine — in Korean the register is baked into the word, so ㅇㅇ to a superior is a politeness error, not just informal

ㄹㅇ.nuance: ㄹㅇ is the consonant skeleton of 리얼, Korea's borrowing of English 'real,' and it works two ways: as a reply it's emphatic agreement ('for real / no joke / facts'), and dropped inside a sentence it's an intensifier meaning 'genuinely/seriously' (이거 ㄹㅇ 웃겨 = 'this is genuinely funny'). It's very current 20-30s slang, at home in friend chats and comments, and frequently fused with ㅋㅋ as ㄹㅇㅋㅋ. Its native-Korean cousins are 진짜 and 정말 ('really/truly'), which carry the same meaning but sound a notch less slangy — and those are what you'd upgrade to in polite contexts (진짜요/정말요). Two English-speaker pitfalls: first, don't decode ㄹㅇ as 'right now' or any English-acronym guess — it's strictly '리얼/real (for real).' Second, ㄹㅇ overlaps heavily with the agreement word ㅇㅈ (인정, 'agreed'), but they aren't identical: ㄹㅇ asserts 'that's TRUE,' while ㅇㅈ concedes 'I ADMIT/agree' — close enough to stack (ㄹㅇ ㅇㅈ) but ㄹㅇ also works as a standalone intensifier where ㅇㅈ can't. And keep it casual: this is young-person slang, so with seniors say 진짜요/정말요, not ㄹㅇ. Note too that position rewrites the meaning — bare ㄹㅇ is 'true,' ㄹㅇ? is 'seriously?!', and mid-sentence ㄹㅇ is just 'really' — so the same two letters do three different jobs.
ㄹㅇ.explanation: ㄹㅇ (rieul-ieung (read as 리얼 / real)) = "for real / fr — short for 리얼 (English 'real'). Means 'seriously / no joke / I agree it's true.' (casual slang — friends and peers, common among young people)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: ㄹㅇ ("for real"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.
ㄹㅇ.shortExplanation: ㄹㅇ is a practical expression meaning "for real / fr — short for 리얼 (English 'real'). Means 'seriously / no joke / I agree it's true.' (casual slang — friends and peers, common among young people)".
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

Treating ㄹㅇ and ㅇㅈ as identical — ㄹㅇ asserts 'that's true / genuinely' (and can intensify mid-sentence), while ㅇㅈ specifically means 'I agree/admit it'; only ㄹㅇ works as a plain intensifier

ㅇㅈ.nuance: ㅇㅈ is the consonant frame of 인정 (Sino-Korean 認定, 'recognize + fix/settle'), literally 'to acknowledge/admit something as so' — and as slang it became young Koreans' punchy way to say 'agreed, that's facts.' Its polite equivalents are 맞아요 ('that's right'), 동의해요 ('I agree'), and very formal 동의합니다, which are what you'd use with seniors. Two English-speaker pitfalls. First, the literal core is 'acknowledge/admit,' so beyond cheerful agreement it can carry a faint flavor of conceding a point ('okay, I'll grant you that') — and the bare-noun 인정 even works as a real verb (그 실수는 인정 = 'I admit that mistake'); reading it as only upbeat 'yes!' misses that edge. Second, don't blur it with ㄹㅇ: ㅇㅈ = 'I agree/admit (인정),' a stance toward what you said; ㄹㅇ = 'for real/genuinely (리얼),' a claim about truth that can also intensify a sentence. They pair (ㄹㅇ ㅇㅈ) but aren't swappable everywhere. As always, keep ㅇㅈ casual — to a boss write 맞습니다 / 동의합니다. And mind the function: ㅇㅈ endorses an OPINION/take, so it fits 'good song / weekdays are better' — it is not a plain factual 'yeah' to a yes/no (that's ㅇㅇ).
ㅇㅈ.explanation: "agreed / true that — short for 인정 (acknowledge/admit). Means 'I agree, that's facts.' (casual slang — friends and peers, very popular with young people)" — that is ㅇㅈ (oj (injeong)). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like ㅇㅈ ("agreed / facts"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

좋아요.nuance: 좋아요 is the 해요체 form of the adjective 좋다 'to be good, nice, likeable', but standing alone as a reply it works as a reaction expression: 'sounds good / I like it / okay, let's do that.' As a response to a suggestion (같이 갈까요? 내일 만날까요?) it's an enthusiastic yes — warmer and more committed than a bare 네, which just confirms. The critical dividing line is 괜찮아요. As a reply to an OFFER, 괜찮아요 usually means 'no thanks, I'm fine as I am' — it's a polite refusal — while 좋아요 means 'yes please.' English 'okay', 'fine', and 'that's good' map onto both of them, which is exactly why beginners accidentally decline the coffee, the bag, or the second helping they actually wanted. If someone offers you something and you want it, say 좋아요 or 네, 주세요; 괜찮아요 will get it taken away. 좋아요 also keeps its plain adjective sense ('it's good/nice': 날씨가 좋아요, 이 카페 좋아요), and it's the Korean name of the social-media Like button — 좋아요(를) 누르다 'to like a post.' Register ladder: 좋아 (banmal) → 좋아요 (polite) → 좋습니다 (formal); 좋네요 reacts in the moment to something in front of you. One caution upward: a bare 좋아요 in reply to a senior's proposal can read as you evaluating their idea, so with a boss the natural answers are 네, 좋습니다 or 네, 그렇게 하겠습니다. The second English-speaker pitfall is the 좋아요 / 좋아해요 split: 좋다 is an ADJECTIVE, so the thing takes 이/가 (김치가 좋아요 'I like kimchi / kimchi is good'), while 좋아하다 is a VERB, so the thing takes 을/를 (김치를 좋아해요 'I like kimchi'). 김치를 좋아요 is simply wrong — pick one pattern and match the particle to it.

It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 좋아요 ("sounds good / I like it"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

Writing 김치를 좋아요 — 좋다 is an adjective and takes 이/가 (김치가 좋아요); the verb 좋아하다 is what takes 을/를 (김치를 좋아해요).
Using a bare 네 where 좋아요 belongs — 네 just confirms you heard, while 좋아요 shows you actually like the idea; to a suggestion, 네 alone can sound lukewarm.

가격 조정.nuance: 가격(價格) is Sino-Korean — 價 'value/price' + 格 'standard' — so it literally means the 'value-standard' set on a thing, the official posted price. Its native-Korean twin is 값, and the line is feel and register: 값 is shorter, warmer, and used in fixed everyday phrases (값이 싸다, 값을 치르다), while 가격 sounds more neutral and 'tag/system' (가격표 price tag, 가격 인상 price hike) and is what you read on signs. The biggest English-speaker trap is the adjective: a high price is 비싸요 (expensive), a low price is 싸요 (cheap) — Koreans do NOT say 가격이 높아요/낮아요 the way English says 'high/low price', so importing 'high' here sounds off. Note too that to ask a clerk you rarely say the noun at all: the natural line is just 얼마예요? ('how much?'). 가격 collocates with 비싸다, 싸다, 오르다 (rise), 내리다 (drop), and 깎다 (haggle down).
가격 조정.explanation: 가격 (gagyeok) means "price". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 가격이 비싸요 ("the price is high"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 가격 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.
가격 조정.shortExplanation: 가격 means "price" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 가격이 높아요 for 'the price is high' — that is a direct translation of English; Korean uses 비싸요 (expensive). Use 높다/낮다 only for height or numbers like temperature, not for prices.
Treating 가격 and 값 as freely swappable — they overlap, but you say 값을 치르다 (pay the price), not 가격을 치르다, and 가격표 (price tag), not 값표. Learn them as set phrases.
Asking a shopkeeper 가격이 뭐예요? ('what is the price?'). The natural question is 얼마예요? or 가격이 얼마예요?, never 뭐예요 for an amount.

ex.note: -(으)며 lists two stages of one process in a single sentence.

신청.nuance: 신청 is a Sino-Korean noun (申請, 申 'state/report' + 請 'request') meaning a formal application or request you put in to an office, bank, or service — you are asking an authority to grant or process something. It overwhelmingly takes 하다 to become the verb 신청하다 ('to apply for'), and 신청서 is the physical form you fill in. Compare it carefully with 지원 (支援/志願): 신청 is the neutral 'put in a request' (카드를 신청하다 = apply for a card), while 지원 is 'apply to/for' a job or school where you are a candidate being selected (회사에 지원하다 = apply to a company). Also distinguish 접수, which is the office's act of RECEIVING and logging your 신청. Register is neutral-to-formal, standard in any official or banking setting. The classic English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 지원 for everyday errands (it sounds like job-hunting) and forgetting that 신청 needs 하다 to act as a verb — 신청 by itself is only the noun, so 'I apply' is 신청해요, not bare 신청.
신청.explanation: "application" is 신청 (sincheong). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 신청을 하다 ("to apply / submit an application"). Watch the particle attached to 신청 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
신청.shortExplanation: 신청 means "application" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 지원 for everyday requests like 'apply for a card' — 지원하다 implies competing for a job/school; for services and paperwork use 신청하다 (카드를 신청해요).
Saying bare 신청 to mean 'I apply' — 신청 is a noun; you must add 하다 (신청해요) or 을/를 하다 (신청을 해요).
Confusing 신청 (your request) with 접수 (the office logging it) — you 신청하다, then the counter 접수하다; they are two sides of one transaction.

usagePhrases.note: 신청 + 하다 is the verb form
으로 marks the method/channel

접수.nuance: 접수 is a Sino-Korean noun (接受, 接 'receive/connect' + 受 'accept') meaning the RECEIVING and logging of an application or document by an office — both the act of an institution taking your submission in, and (loosely) your act of handing it in at the 접수 창구 (intake window). It takes 하다 and 되다: from your side 서류를 접수하다 can mean 'submit/file', while 접수가 되다 / 접수되다 means 'it has been received/registered by them'. The crucial trio for learners: 신청 (you REQUEST) → 접수 (the office RECEIVES/logs it) → 처리 (處理, they PROCESS it). So 접수 sits in the middle, the moment your paperwork is officially accepted and assigned a 접수 번호. Distinguish it from 제출 (提出, the physical act of 'submitting/handing over' a document) — 제출 is the handing in, 접수 is the institution accepting and registering it. Register is neutral-formal, standard at hospitals, offices, and event desks (병원 접수 = hospital reception/check-in). The English-speaker pitfall is treating 접수 as plain 'submit' (that is 제출) and missing its 'be accepted/logged' meaning — 접수가 됐어요 means your application is now officially in the system, not merely handed over.
접수.explanation: 접수 (jeopsu) = "reception, filing". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 접수를 하다 ("to file/submit (and have it logged)") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 접수, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
접수.shortExplanation: 접수 means "reception, filing" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 접수 as just 'submit' — 제출 is handing the document over; 접수 is the office RECEIVING and logging it (접수되다 = it's now registered).
Confusing 접수 (intake/logging) with 등록 (being entered on the register) — 접수 comes first at the desk; 등록 is the later formal record.
Reading 병원 접수 as 'hospital application' — here 접수 is the reception/check-in desk where you register your visit.

되다 = the office has logged it
the counter that takes submissions
the number assigned when filed

서류.nuance: 서류 is a Sino-Korean noun (書類, 書 'writing/document' + 類 'kind/category') meaning official documents or paperwork as a category — the bundle of forms, copies, and certificates a procedure demands. It is a collective, somewhat abstract term: 서류를 준비하다 = get your paperwork in order, covering many individual papers at once. Contrast it with 문서 (文書), which is 'a document' as a discrete file or record (often electronic or archival, e.g. an internal 문서), while 서류 evokes the practical stack you submit for an application. A single sheet is 종이 (paper) and one specific form is e.g. 신청서; 서류 is the umbrella. Natural collocations are 서류를 준비하다/챙기다/제출하다/접수하다 and 서류 심사 (document review). Register is neutral, ubiquitous at banks, immigration, and government offices. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 서류 as countable like 'a document' — Korean uses it as a mass/collective noun, so you rarely say 한 서류; for one item name the specific form (신청서 한 장) or use 문서 for a discrete record.
서류.explanation: 서류 (seoryu) means "documents". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 서류를 준비하다 ("to prepare the documents"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 서류 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
서류.shortExplanation: 서류 means "documents" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting it like English 'a document' (한 서류) — 서류 is collective/mass; for one sheet say 신청서 한 장 or 서류 한 부 (one set).
Swapping 서류 and 문서 freely — 서류 is the practical paperwork you submit; 문서 is a discrete document/file, often archival or electronic.
Using 종이 for official papers — 종이 is the physical material 'paper'; the forms and certificates you submit are 서류.

제출하다 = hand them in

등록.nuance: 등록 is a Sino-Korean noun (登錄, 登 'record/ascend' + 錄 'register/record') meaning officially entering a person or thing onto a register or roll — enrolling, registering, recording in a system. It takes 하다 (등록하다 = to register) or 되다 (등록되다 = to be registered), and appears in 외국인 등록증 (alien registration card), 주민등록 (resident registration), 등록금 (registration/tuition fee), 등록 번호 (registration number). The contrast learners need is with 신청 and 접수: 신청 is REQUESTING something, 접수 is the office RECEIVING your request, and 등록 is the result of being formally ENTERED onto the official record — often you 신청 first, the desk 접수, and finally you are 등록 in the system. Compare also 가입 (加入, 'joining/subscribing' to a membership, service, or insurance — 보험 가입, 회원 가입), which is about becoming a MEMBER, whereas 등록 is about being recorded in a registry. Register is neutral-formal. The English-speaker pitfall is using 등록 for joining a club or signing up for a service (that is 가입) and using 가입 for recording an official entry (that is 등록) — and remembering 등록 needs 하다/되다 to function as a verb.
등록.explanation: "registration" is 등록 (deungnok). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 등록을 하다 ("to register"). Watch the particle attached to 등록 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
등록.shortExplanation: 등록 means "registration" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

Using 등록 for joining a membership or service — that is 가입 (회원 가입); 등록 is being entered on an official register.
Confusing 등록 with 신청 — you 신청하다 (request) something first; 등록 is the resulting formal entry in the records.
Saying bare 등록 as a verb — add 하다 (등록해요) or 되다 (등록됐어요); 등록 alone is only the noun.

첨부.nuance: 첨부 means attaching a file to a message, and 첨부 파일 (attached file) is one of the highest-frequency phrases in Korean work email. It is Sino-Korean 添附, literally 'add-attach', both characters meaning to append something extra. The distinction to keep is digital 첨부하다 (attach an email file) vs physical 붙이다 (stick/glue something to a surface) vs 부착하다 (affix a label/poster) — English says 'attach' for all three, but a file is only ever 첨부하다. Its fixed companion line 첨부 파일을 확인해 주세요 is basically email etiquette you can paste anywhere. The English-speaker pitfall, beyond reaching for 붙이다, is spacing: in careful business writing it is two words, 첨부 파일, not 첨부파일 (though the squished form is tolerated in casual chat). Also note 첨부 has no plain past on its own — you write 첨부했어요/첨부했습니다, never 첨부 했어요 with a gap.
첨부.explanation: "attachment (file); attaching" is 첨부 (cheombu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 파일을 첨부하다 ("to attach a file"). Watch the particle attached to 첨부 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.
첨부.shortExplanation: 첨부 means "attachment (file); attaching" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

Saying 파일을 붙이다 ('stick the file') from English 'attach' — physical sticking is 붙이다, but an email file is 첨부하다

Saying 첨부 파일을 보다 to ask the reader to look — politely you say 확인해 주세요 ('please confirm/check'); plain 보다 sounds like a bare command

ex.note: 보도되다 is the 되다 passive: the outlets do it, but they are not the subject.

보도.nuance: 보도 is Sino-Korean, 步道, literally 'step-road' (步 walk + 道 road) — the formal name for the pedestrian walkway beside a street, identical in meaning to 인도 (人道, 'person-road'). The dividing line between the two is register and channel: 보도 dominates official signage and traffic law (보도 침범 = encroaching on the sidewalk), while 인도 is what people more often say in casual speech; both are correct. Its true opposite is 차도 (車道, 'car-road', the roadway). The everyday compound 보도블록 (the tiled paving blocks) comes up constantly in complaints about uneven sidewalks. The big English-speaker pitfall is a homograph collision: another 보도 means 'news report' (報道, as in 언론 보도 = press coverage) — same hangul, different hanja — so a sentence about 보도 could be about pavement or the press, and only context tells them apart. Also note British 'pavement' = American 'sidewalk' = 보도; don't read it as the road surface.
보도.explanation: 보도 (bodo) = "sidewalk / pavement". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 보도로 걷다 ("to walk on the sidewalk") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 보도, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.
보도.shortExplanation: 보도 means "sidewalk / pavement" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 보도 (步道, the pedestrian sidewalk) with 차도 (車道, the roadway for cars) — they are opposites; walking on the 차도 is dangerous
Reading 보도 as 'news report' — that is the homograph 報道 (報 report + 道); the street sense is 步道, so let context decide
For British speakers, do not treat 'pavement' as the road surface — 보도 is the raised walkway pedestrians use, equal to American 'sidewalk'

usagePhrases.note: 로 = along/by
위 = on top of/along
describing it
the tiled blocks underfoot

examples.en: Walk on the sidewalk.
examples.note: the simplest safety instruction; 로 = along/by way of

examples.en: The sidewalk was narrow, so we walked single file.
examples.note: 아서 = because; a real everyday observation about Korean sidewalks

examples.en: A bike was riding on the sidewalk, so it was almost dangerous.
examples.note: ㄹ 뻔했다 = nearly happened; the live issue of bikes on 보도

ex.ko: 정부는 지원을 확대하겠다고 밝혔다.
ex.en: The government stated that it will expand support.
ex.note: -다고 밝혔다 is how news quotes an official statement. Its passive is 밝혀지다.

ex.ko: 정부에 따르면 이번 조치는 내년 상반기에 시행된다.
ex.en: According to the government, this measure takes effect in the first half of next year.
ex.note: N에 따르면 introduces the source, and 시행되다 keeps the actor out.

정부.nuance: 정부 (政府, 政 'governing/administration' + 府 'office/seat of authority' — literally the 'office of governance') is the government as the concrete administrative body that runs the state. The contrast to lock in is 정부 vs 정치: 정부 is the institution/body, while 정치 (politics) is the activity and field — '정부가 발표했어요' (the body announced) but '정치에 관심 없어요' (not interested in the field). A grammar point unique to organizational subjects: Korean lets you mark 정부 as the actor with 에서 as well as 가 — both 정부에서 발표했어요 and 정부가 발표했어요 are correct, with 에서 feeling a touch more formal/institutional. Pair 정부 with official verbs: 발표하다, 결정하다, 지원하다, 추진하다.
정부.explanation: 정부 (jeongbu) means "government". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 정부 정책 ("government policy"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 정부 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
정부.shortExplanation: 정부 means "government" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 정부 with 정치. 정부 is the governing body (정부가 결정하다); 정치 is the field/activity (정치를 하다, 정치에 관심이 있다).
Assuming organizational subjects only take 가. With bodies like 정부, the 에서 form is equally natural: 정부에서 발표했어요 ≈ 정부가 발표했어요.

usagePhrases.note: Extremely common in news; 정부 modifies the noun directly with no 의.
발표하다 is the standard verb for official statements by the 정부.
The standard administrative split between national and regional authority.
Heard constantly about funding, benefits, and aid (정부 지원을 받다 = receive government support).

examples.en: The government announced a new policy.
examples.note: Core news frame: 정부 + 발표하다, the textbook subject-verb pairing.

examples.ko: 많은 사람들이 정부의 결정에 반대하고 있어요.
examples.romanization: maneun saramdeuri jeongbuui gyeoljeonge bandaehago isseoyo.
examples.en: Many people are opposing the government's decision.
examples.note: 정부의 결정 uses 의 to link two nouns; 반대하다 takes 에 (결정에 반대하다).

examples.ko: 정부에서 소상공인을 위한 지원을 늘리기로 했어요.
examples.romanization: jeongbueseo sosanggongineul wihan jiwoneul neulligiro haesseoyo.
examples.en: The government decided to increase support for small business owners.
examples.note: 정부에서: organizations as subjects often take 에서, which sounds slightly more institutional than 가.

ex.ko: 지원 대상이 다음 달부터 확대된다.
ex.en: The range of recipients expands from next month.
ex.note: 확대하다 is transitive; a thing that expands on its own takes 확대되다.

확대.nuance: 확대 uses 대 as big: the thing becomes larger in size or scope.
확대.explanation: 확대 (hwakdae) = "expansion; enlargement". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 화면 확대 ("screen enlargement") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 확대, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
확대.shortExplanation: 확대 means "expansion; enlargement" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
확대 is not the same as 대단하다; 대단하다 praises something as impressive.

usagePhrases.note: making something bigger

examples.en: If the letters are small, try enlarging the screen.
examples.note: 확대 is making the scale bigger.

ex.ko: 이용객 수가 지난해보다 증가한 것으로 나타났다.
ex.en: Passenger numbers were found to have risen compared with last year.
ex.note: -(으)ㄴ 것으로 나타나다: 'was found to have', a standard reporting frame.

ex.ko: 생산 공정이 자동화되면서 인력 수요가 크게 감소했다.
ex.en: As the production process was automated, demand for workers fell sharply.
ex.note: 자동화되다 and 감소하다 — the 화 suffix and its usual consequence.

ex.ko: 올해 물가가 더 오를 것으로 전망된다.
ex.en: Prices are forecast to rise further this year.
ex.note: -(으)ㄹ 것으로 전망된다 is the fixed forecast frame.

ex.ko: 복구 작업은 이달 말까지 이어질 예정이다.
ex.en: Recovery work is scheduled to continue until the end of this month.
ex.note: -(으)ㄹ 예정이다 states a plan; notices shorten it to 예정임.

ex.ko: 안전 기준 강화의 필요성이 크다는 지적이 이어지고 있다.
ex.en: Criticism continues that there is a strong need to tighten safety standards.
ex.note: 필요성 takes 크다, unlike 가능성, which takes 높다.

ex.ko: 제도 변화가 시장에 미칠 영향이 주목되고 있다.
ex.en: The effect the change in the system will have on the market is drawing attention.
ex.note: 변화 is itself a 화 word: 변 plus 화, 'becoming different'.

변화.nuance: 변화 (變化, '變 to alter + 化 to transform' — alteration-and-transformation) is the noun 'change', used for shifts in states, trends, weather, society, technology, or one's life, and it is more abstract and global than the plain verb 변하다/바뀌다 (a specific thing changes). Distinguish 변화를 주다 ('introduce/make a change', usually for freshness or variety) from 변화가 생기다 ('a change occurs' on its own), and mark what you adapt to with 에 (변화에 적응하다). The subtle English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 변화하다 as the verb for everyday change: 변화하다 exists but sounds formal/scientific ('the climate is changing' 기후가 변화하다), so for ordinary 'something changed' use 변하다 or 바뀌다 (전화번호가 바뀌었어요 'my number changed'), and reserve 변화 for the noun. Compare 발전 (發展, development/progress — change specifically in a better, advancing direction), which carries positive growth that neutral 변화 does not.
변화.explanation: 변화 (byeonhwa) = "change". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 변화가 생기다 ("a change occurs") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 변화, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
변화.shortExplanation: 변화 means "change" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Use the verb 변하다/바뀌다 for ordinary 'something changes'; the noun-verb 변화하다 sounds formal/scientific, so 전화번호가 바뀌었어요, not 전화번호가 변화했어요.
Say 변화를 주다 ('make/introduce a change') in the 'add variety' sense, not 변화를 하다.
Don't use neutral 변화 when you mean improvement: positive, advancing change is 발전 (회사가 발전했어요), while 변화 is direction-neutral.

usagePhrases.note: the natural intransitive way to say a change arises; subject takes 이/가
분위기에 변화를 주다 = add a change to the mood/atmosphere
modified by 급격한/큰/작은 to describe scale and speed
the thing you adapt to takes 에: 변화에 적응하다

examples.en: These days the weather changes a lot.
examples.note: Simple: 변화가 심하다 = the change is severe/big

examples.ko: 기분 전환하려고 머리 스타일에 변화를 줬어요.
examples.romanization: gibun jeonhwanharyeogo meori seutaire byeonhwareul jwosseoyo.
examples.en: I changed up my hairstyle for a change of mood.
examples.note: Everyday: 변화를 주다 = deliberately introduce a change for variety

examples.ko: 새로운 환경의 변화에 적응하는 데 거의 반년이 걸렸어요.
examples.romanization: saeroun hwangyeongui byeonhwae jeogeunghaneun de geoui bannyeoni geollyeosseoyo.
examples.en: It took nearly half a year to adapt to the changes of the new environment.
examples.note: Real situation: 변화에 적응하다 over a realistic adjustment period

ex.ko: 이번 조치가 물가에 미친 영향은 아직 크지 않은 것으로 분석됐다.
ex.en: The effect of this measure on prices is analysed as not yet significant.
ex.note: 영향을 미치다 is the fixed collocation, not 영향을 주다 in formal writing.

영향.nuance: 영향 (影響, '影 shadow + 響 echo' — a shadow-and-echo that one thing casts onto another) is influence or impact, and it crucially works in two opposite directions you must keep straight: the source 영향을 주다 / 미치다 (gives/exerts an effect) while the recipient 영향을 받다 (receives/is affected). 미치다 is the formal, news-and-essay verb for 'exert an effect', whereas 주다 is everyday conversation. The decisive English-speaker trap is the particle: the affected target is marked with 에 (for things — 환경에 영향을 주다) or 에게/께 (for people — 아이들에게/부모님께 영향을 주다), NOT with 을/를, because the actual object slot is already filled by 영향(을). So 'it affects the environment' is 환경에 영향을 줘요, never 환경을 영향을 줘요. Compare 효과 (效果, the resulting effect/efficacy of a measure, e.g. 약의 효과 'the medicine's effect'): 영향 is the act of influencing, 효과 is the beneficial result that comes out.
영향.explanation: 영향 (yeonghyang) means "influence, effect, impact". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 영향을 주다 ("give influence, affect"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 영향 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
영향.shortExplanation: 영향 means "influence, effect, impact" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't swap the direction: the affecter uses 주다/미치다, the affected uses 받다. '나는 영향을 줬어요' means YOU influenced something, not that you were influenced.
Mark the target with 에 (things) or 에게/께 (people), not 을/를: 환경에 영향을 주다, never 환경을 영향을 주다.
Don't use 영향 for the beneficial 'effect' of a remedy — that is 효과 (약의 효과); 영향 is the broader, often neutral act of influencing.

usagePhrases.note: X이/가 Y에/에게 영향을 주다 = X affects Y; everyday register
X에게서/에서 영향을 받다 = to be affected by X; the receiving side
more formal than 주다; standard in writing and news
modified by 좋은/나쁜/큰 to describe the effect's quality and size

examples.en: The weather affects my mood.
examples.note: Simple: N에 영향을 주다 — the affected target takes 에, not 을/를

examples.ko: 저는 어릴 때 할머니께 많은 영향을 받았어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun eoril ttae halmeonikke maneun yeonghyangeul badasseoyo.
examples.en: I was greatly influenced by my grandmother when I was little.
examples.note: Everyday: 영향을 받다 with 께 for the respected person who influenced you

examples.ko: 이번 정책은 자영업자들에게 큰 영향을 미칠 것으로 보입니다.
examples.romanization: ibeon jeongchaegeun jayeongeopjadeurege keun yeonghyangeul michil geoseuro boimnida.
examples.en: This policy is expected to have a big impact on the self-employed.
examples.note: Real situation: formal 영향을 미치다 in news/report register

ex.ko: 시장에서는 가격이 더 오를 것으로 예상된다는 반응이 나왔다.
ex.en: The market reaction was that prices are expected to rise further.
ex.note: 예상되다 keeps the forecaster anonymous — standard in market reporting.

시장.nuance: 시장 (市場, 'market-place/field') is an open traditional market: rows of small independent stalls selling produce, fish, side dishes and clothes, where prices are flexible and you can haggle. The dividing line from its near-synonym 마트 is atmosphere and pricing — 마트 is a single fixed-price corporate store, while 시장 is many vendors and bargaining (깎다) is normal. Don't confuse it with 장 alone (which in 장을 보다 / 장날 means the shopping or market-day event) or with the homophone 시장 (市長, 'mayor'); only context tells them apart. The classic English-speaker trap is the particle: you say 시장에 가요 for *going there* (에 = destination) but 시장에서 사요 for *buying there* (에서 = where the action happens), and English 'go shopping' becomes the fixed idiom 시장을 보다, using 보다 'see', never 사다.
시장.explanation: 시장 (sijang) means "traditional market". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 전통 시장 ("a traditional market"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 시장 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then change a single part.
시장.shortExplanation: 시장 means "traditional market" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 시장에서 가요 for 'I go to the market'. With the movement verb 가다 you need the destination particle 에 (시장에 가요); 에서 would wrongly mean an action performed *at* the market.
Translating 'go shopping' word-for-word as 시장을 사요. The fixed expression is 시장을 보다 ('see the market'); 사다 needs a specific object like 과일을 사요.
Mixing up 시장(市場, market) and 시장(市長, mayor) because they sound identical. They are different words; rely on context — 시장에 가다 = market, 시장님 = mayor.

usagePhrases.note: The set phrase Koreans use to distinguish an old open-air market from a modern store; 전통 = 'tradition'.
에 marks the destination you move toward; pair it with movement verbs 가다/오다/다니다.
에서 marks where an action takes place; here the buying happens inside the market.
An idiom: 시장(을) 보다 literally 'see the market' but means to go shopping for groceries — note 보다, not 사다.

examples.en: The market is big.
examples.note: A bare description; subject particle 이 after a consonant. Start simple.

examples.en: Every weekend I buy fruit at the traditional market.
examples.note: 마다 = 'every'; 에서 because the buying happens at the market, not 에.

examples.ko: 시장에 가면 깎아 달라고 해 보세요.
examples.romanization: sijange gamyeon kkakka dallago hae boseyo.
examples.en: When you go to the market, try asking them to knock the price down.
examples.note: 깎다 = 'cut/discount the price' — real bargaining only happens at 시장, not at a fixed-price 마트.

ex.ko: 피해가 큰 지역부터 복구 작업이 본격화될 예정이다.
ex.en: Recovery work is scheduled to begin in earnest in the worst-hit areas first.
ex.note: 본격화되다 plus -(으)ㄹ 예정이다 — two news frames stacked.

지역.nuance: 지역 is Sino-Korean 地域 ('land/earth' 地 + 'boundary/territory' 域), a bounded geographic area, and by extension the 지역 사회 (local community). Two contrasts matter. Against 지방(地方) 'the provinces': 지역 is any neutral region (수도권 지역 included), whereas 지방 specifically means everywhere OUTSIDE Seoul (지방에 살다 = to live in the provinces), often with a center-vs-rest nuance. Against 동네: 지역 is formal/administrative (지역 경제, 지역 주민), while 동네 is your warm, familiar block where neighbors know you. Register is neutral-formal, common in news and policy. English-speaker pitfall: 'I'm from the countryside/regions' becomes 지방, not 지역; and your cozy neighborhood is 동네, so '우리 동네' (my neighborhood) sounds natural where '우리 지역' would feel like a press release.
지역.explanation: 지역 (jiyeok) means "region; area; local district". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 이 지역 ("this area/region"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 지역 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
지역.shortExplanation: 지역 means "region; area; local district" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 지역 (any neutral region/area) with 지방 — 지방 specifically means the provinces outside the capital ('지방 출신' = from outside Seoul).
Using 지역 for your cozy neighborhood — that warmer, personal sense is 동네 (우리 동네 빵집).
Saying 지역이 크다 for community closeness — for a tight-knit local society use 지역 사회, and describe size of land with 넓다 (wide), not just 크다.

usagePhrases.note: Common demonstrative + 지역, for any defined locale.
주민(住民) = residents; the set pairing in civic talk.
사회(社會) = society; 지역 사회 = the local community as a whole.
수도권(首都圈) = the greater-Seoul metropolitan zone.

examples.en: This area is quiet.
examples.note: Simple description; 지역 as a neutral 'area' you can point to on a map.

examples.en: Dialects and food differ a little from region to region.
examples.note: Everyday observation; 지역마다 = every region, 사투리 = dialect, 조금씩 = bit by bit.

examples.ko: 지역 주민들이 환경 보호 활동에 적극적으로 참여했어요.
examples.romanization: jiyeok jumindeuri hwangyeong boho hwaldonge jeokgeukjeogeuro chamyeohaesseoyo.
examples.en: Local residents actively took part in environmental protection activities.
examples.note: Civic-news register; 적극적으로 = actively, 참여하다 = to participate, -에 marks the activity.

ex.ko: 어머니는 손이 크셔서 늘 음식을 넉넉히 하세요.
ex.en: My mother does things on such a scale that she always makes plenty of food.
ex.note: 손이 크다 is about generosity, never about the size of anyone's hand.

손.nuance: 손 is the hand, and the first thing to fix is the washing verb: hands take 씻다 (손을 씻다), in deliberate contrast to hair, which uses 감다 — mixing them (손을 감다) is a classic beginner slip. Beyond the literal organ, 손 powers vivid idioms that aren't about anatomy: 손이 크다 ('big hand') means generous, especially someone who cooks or gives a lot, not someone with large hands; 손이 가다 ('the hand goes') means a task or person takes a lot of effort/attention; and 손이 모자라다 ('hands are short') means short-staffed. To hold someone's hand is 손을 잡다 (잡다 = grasp), used both romantically and to guide a child across the road. Note the hand is usually the object of an action, so it pairs with 을/를 (손을 씻다, 손을 잡다) rather than 가.
손.explanation: 손 (son) = "hand". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 손을 씻다 ("to wash one's hands") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 손, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.
손.shortExplanation: 손 means "hand" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 손을 감다 for washing hands — 감다 is reserved for hair; hands use 씻다, so 손을 씻다.
Reading 손이 크다 as literally big hands — it idiomatically means generous/open-handed, often about serving lots of food.
Saying 손을 들다 when you mean hold hands — 손을 들다 is to raise your hand (to answer); holding hands is 손을 잡다.

발.nuance: 발 is specifically the foot — the part below the ankle — and Korean keeps it strictly separate from 다리 (the leg, the whole limb above), so pointing at your ankle and saying 다리 is wrong; that is the core mix-up for English speakers who blur 'leg/foot'. Useful collocations: 발을 다치다 (injure the foot, with 다치다 taking 을/를) and 발이 붓다 (the foot swells), where 붓다 is a ㅅ-irregular verb that drops ㅅ before a vowel → 부어요, 부었어요, not 붓어요. Idiomatically 발이 넓다 ('wide foot') means well-connected with a broad social network, never literally big feet (for that you'd say 발이 크다). When you cause an injury yourself, prefer the active 다치다 (발을 다쳤어요) over a passive construction.
발.explanation: 발 (bal) means "foot". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 발이 아프다 ("one's foot hurts"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 발 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.
발.shortExplanation: 발 means "foot" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 다리 to point at your foot/ankle — 다리 is the whole leg; the foot below the ankle is 발.
Conjugating 붓다 as 붓어요 — it is ㅅ-irregular, so the swelling form is 부어요 / 부었어요.
Reading 발이 넓다 as having big feet — it idiomatically means having wide social connections; big feet is 발이 크다.

입.nuance: 입 is the mouth, but its most useful expressions are idioms that won't survive word-for-word translation. 입에 맞다 means food 'suits your taste' (lit. 'fits the mouth') — it judges flavor, so 'this fits in my mouth' is a beginner mistranslation. 입이 짧다 ('short mouth') describes a picky or light eater, while 입이 무겁다 ('heavy mouth') means tight-lipped/discreet and 입이 가볍다 ('light mouth') means a blabbermouth — none are about physical size. To physically open the mouth is 입을 벌리다 (벌리다 = spread apart), as a dentist commands; do not use 열다 ('open' a door/box) for the mouth. Note also that 입 (mouth, the organ) is different from 말 (speech/words), so 'watch your mouth' as in language is 말조심하다, not anything with 입.

Saying 입을 열다 for opening your mouth at the dentist — 열다 is for doors/boxes; the body uses 입을 벌리다.
Reading 입이 무겁다 as a heavy/big mouth — it idiomatically means discreet and tight-lipped, the opposite of talkative.

examples.ko: 우리 아이는 입이 짧아서 골고루 안 먹어요.

ex.ko: 할머니는 귀가 밝으셔서 작은 소리도 다 들으세요.
ex.en: My grandmother has sharp hearing and catches even the faintest sound.
ex.note: 귀가 밝다 is about hearing — a different pair from 귀가 얇다.

귀.nuance: 귀 is the ear, and the key English-speaker pitfall is the verb of hearing. Korean splits 듣다 (to listen actively, by choice) from 들리다 (to be heard / reach the ear, passively, beyond control). So 'I can't hear' is 귀가 안 들려요 with the passive 들리다 — using 못 듣다 implies you deliberately didn't listen, which is rude when talking about someone's deafness. There are two natural ways to describe hard-of-hearing: the plain 귀가 안 들리다 and the gentler idiom 귀가 어둡다 ('the ear is dark'), whose opposite 귀가 밝다 ('bright ear') means keen hearing. To plug your ears against noise is 귀를 막다 (막다 = block), the same 막다 as a blocked nose (코가 막히다). When speaking about elders, pair this with honorifics, e.g. 귀가 어두우세요.
귀.explanation: "ear" is 귀 (gwi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 귀가 아프다 ("one's ear hurts"). Watch the particle attached to 귀 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.
귀.shortExplanation: 귀 means "ear" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 저는 못 들어요 to mean you are deaf — 못 듣다 implies refusing to listen; for not being able to hear, say 귀가 안 들려요.
Using active 듣다 for involuntary hearing — 'I can hear music' is 음악이 들려요, with passive 들리다.
Saying 귀를 닫다 for covering ears — 닫다 is for doors; to block ears against noise use 귀를 막다.

막다 = block; against loud noise

ex.ko: 그렇게 부탁해 놓고 또 오다니, 얼굴이 두껍네요.
ex.en: Turning up again after asking for all that — what nerve.
ex.note: 얼굴이 두껍다 means shameless, the same image as English 'thick-skinned'.

얼굴.nuance: 얼굴 is the whole human face — both its looks and its surface you wash — and is the everyday word with no formality issue; you use it equally with friends and elders. Its near-synonym 낯 (as in 낯이 익다 'the face looks familiar', 낯설다 'unfamiliar') is old-fashioned and survives mostly in set idioms, so for plain 'face' always reach for 얼굴. Two pitfalls trip up English speakers. First, hair on the head is 감다 (감다 = wash hair) but the FACE is 씻다, the same verb as for hands and dishes — never say 얼굴을 감다. Second, English 'big face' does not transfer: a flattering 'small face' is 얼굴이 작다 (a real Korean compliment about proportion), and you do not say 얼굴이 커요 to mean handsome. Color uses 빨갛다 (얼굴이 빨개요), and to feel for fever Koreans touch the 이마, not the whole 얼굴.
얼굴.explanation: 얼굴 (eolgul) = "face". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 얼굴이 예뻐요 ("the face is pretty") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 얼굴, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.
얼굴.shortExplanation: 얼굴 means "face" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 얼굴을 감다 to mean 'wash my face' — 감다 is only for washing HAIR; the face takes 씻다, so it must be 얼굴을 씻어요.
Translating 'pretty face' as 얼굴이 이뻐다 with wrong spelling; the standard adjective is 예쁘다 → 예뻐요 (the ㅡ drops before -어요).
Using 얼굴이 커요 expecting it to sound flattering — in Korean a large face is unflattering; the compliment is 얼굴이 작다, 'small-faced'.

빨갛다, a ㅎ-irregular, drops ㅎ before -아요
씻다 for water-washing, object particle 을

examples.note: describing looks; possessive 언니 얼굴 needs no 의 in speech

examples.en: I get up in the morning and wash my face.
examples.note: note the verb 씻다, never 감다, takes the object 얼굴을

ex.ko: 머리가 좋은 것보다 꾸준한 게 더 중요해요.
ex.en: Being consistent matters more than being clever.
ex.note: 머리가 좋다 is 'smart'; 머리가 아프다 covers both a headache and a hassle.

머리.nuance: 머리 covers both the head and the hair on it, and only context (the verb or adjective) tells them apart: 머리가 아프다 = head hurts, but 머리가 길다 / 머리를 감다 = hair. The strict word for a single strand is 머리카락, yet in speech Koreans almost always shorten it to 머리, so 'cut my hair' is 머리를 자르다, not 머리카락을 자르다. The pitfall for English speakers is the washing verb: hair takes 감다 (머리를 감다), never the 씻다 you use for hands or face, so 머리를 씻다 sounds childish or wrong. Also note 머리가 좋다/나쁘다 is a fixed idiom for being smart/dim, not a comment on hair quality, and the body part is always marked with 가 (머리가 아파요), not 을.
머리.explanation: 머리 (meori) means "head; also hair". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 머리가 아파요 ("my head hurts"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 머리 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.
머리.shortExplanation: 머리 means "head; also hair" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 머리를 씻다 for washing hair — hair uses the special verb 감다, so the natural form is 머리를 감다.
Saying 머리카락을 자르다 at a salon — it is technically correct but stiff; native speakers just say 머리를 자르다.
Using 머리를 아파요 — a body-part ache marks the part with 가, so it must be 머리가 아파요.

usagePhrases.note: the single most common '머리' complaint; 가 marks the body part
하다 sense of 'hair'; say this at a salon, not 머리카락을 자르다

examples.en: My hair is long.

examples.en: I got a haircut and dyed it at the salon too.

ex.ko: 코가 높은 사람은 먼저 다가가기가 좀 어려워요.
ex.en: Someone haughty is a little hard to approach first.
ex.note: 코가 높다 means haughty; save it for people who are not in the room.

코.nuance: 코 is the nose, but cold symptoms split into precise collocations English speakers must memorize: a blocked nose is 코가 막히다 (막히다 = be blocked) and a runny nose is 콧물이 나다, where 콧물 literally stitches 코(nose)+물(water) into 'nose-water' = snot. Saying 코가 아프다 actually means the nose physically hurts (an injury), so it does NOT convey a cold — that is the classic 직역 trap. To blow your nose is 코를 풀다 (풀다 'to release/undo'); beware 코를 불다, which means to blow air out like a whistle and sounds absurd here. For looks, a tall nose bridge (admired in Korea) is 코가 높다, with 코가 낮다 as the flat-bridge opposite, paralleling how 키가 크다 works for height.
코.explanation: 코 (ko) = "nose". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 코가 막히다 ("to have a stuffy nose") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 코, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Saying 코가 아파요 to mean you have a cold — that means literal nose pain; use 코가 막혀요 (stuffy) or 콧물이 나요 (runny).
Saying 코를 불다 for blowing your nose — 불다 is blowing air out; the correct verb is 풀다, so 코를 풀다.
Using just 코가 나다 for a runny nose — you need the compound 콧물; say 콧물이 나요.

usagePhrases.note: the standard cold symptom; 막히다 = be blocked
for snot use the compound 콧물 (코+물), not just 코
풀다 'release'; never 코를 불다 (that is whistling/blowing air)

ex.ko: 성격이 급해서 손이 빠른 대신 실수도 잦아요.
ex.en: I'm impatient, so I work fast but also make frequent mistakes.
ex.note: 손이 빠르다 — quick-handed — is another member of the 손 family.

성격.nuance: 성격 (性格, 性 'nature/disposition' + 格 'character/frame') is a person's enduring inborn character — the stable temperament you are born with and keep for life. Contrast it carefully with 기분, which is a passing mood that changes hourly: '오늘 기분이 좋아요' = I'm in a good mood today (temporary), whereas '성격이 좋아요' = he's a good-natured person (permanent). Mixing these is the single most common error: never use 성격 for how you feel right now. The phrase 성격이 좋다 is a warm social compliment meaning kind, tolerant, easy to get along with — broader than English 'good personality'. Note also 성격이 급하다 ('impatient/hot-tempered nature') is an idiomatic fixed expression. Common partner adjectives: 밝다 (cheerful), 활발하다 (lively), 조용하다 (quiet), 까다롭다 (fussy/picky), 무뚝뚝하다 (blunt). Pitfall beyond the 기분 trap: 'I have a ~ personality' is most naturally 성격이 + adjective (성격이 밝아요), not the heavier 저는 ~한 성격을 가지고 있어요 calque, though 급한 성격이에요 is fine.
성격.explanation: "personality" is 성격 (seonggyeok). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 제 성격은 조용해요. ("My personality is quiet."). Watch the particle attached to 성격 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
성격.shortExplanation: 성격 means "personality" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 성격 for a temporary mood: 오늘 성격이 좋아요 wrongly says 'my permanent character is good today'. For mood use 기분: 오늘 기분이 좋아요.
Calquing 'have a good personality' as 성격을 가지고 있어요. Korean states it with an adjective: 성격이 좋아요 or 성격이 밝아요.
Confusing 성격 with 성질. 성질 also means temperament but skews negative/temper-flare ('성질을 내다' = lose one's temper). To neutrally describe character, use 성격.

성격이 좋다 = 'is good-natured/easygoing', a common compliment
성격이 비슷하다 compares two people's natures
밝다 ('bright') applied to 성격 = cheerful and warm

ex.en: He's discreet, so I feel safe trusting him with a secret.
ex.note: 비밀을 맡기다 and 비밀을 지키다 are the two standard collocations.

비밀.nuance: 비밀 (祕密, 祕 'hidden/mysterious' + 密 'dense/close') paints a secret as something kept tightly closed in. The verb it lives with is 지키다 ('to guard/keep'), giving 비밀을 지키다 — note that English 'keep a secret' tempts learners to reach for 가지다 ('to have/hold'), but 비밀을 가지다 sounds wrong; you 지키다 (guard) a secret, or 비밀로 하다 (make it secret). Contrast 비밀 with 비결: both share 비(祕), but 비결 (祕訣) is a 'secret know-how / the trick to success' (성공의 비결 = the secret to success), not confidential information. So a chef's 비결 is their technique, while their 비밀 might be that they hate cooking. The word is register-neutral and used freely from children's games to government affairs. Pitfall to avoid: 비밀 is a noun only — there is no verb 비밀하다. To say 'keep something secret' you must add a verb: 비밀로 하다 or 비밀을 지키다.
비밀.explanation: "secret" is 비밀 (bimil). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 이것은 비밀이에요. ("This is a secret."). Watch the particle attached to 비밀 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
비밀.shortExplanation: 비밀 means "secret" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 비밀 as a verb: 비밀해요 does not exist. Use 비밀로 해요 (make it secret) or 비밀을 지켜요 (keep the secret).
Saying 비밀을 가지다 by translating 'have/keep a secret' literally. Korean guards a secret: 비밀을 지키다. To say you simply possess secrets, use 비밀이 있다 / 없다.
Mixing up 비밀 (confidential info) and 비결 (the secret trick/know-how). 'The secret to long life' is 장수의 비결, not 장수의 비밀.

비밀을 지키다 = 'protect/guard a secret', the standard collocation
비밀이 없다 with the subject particle states you hide nothing
비밀로 하다 = 'treat it as secret'; -로 marks the resulting state

examples.note: 한테 marks the human recipient you told it to

ex.note: 마음에 들다 is itself an idiom: 'it enters the heart' = you like it.

마음.nuance: 마음 is the native word for the heart-mind: the seat of feelings, will, intentions, and disposition — never the physical organ (that is 심장 心臟, the pump). Contrast it with 생각 (thought/idea, the cognitive content) and with 기분 (a passing mood): 마음 is the deeper, more stable inner self where kindness, sincerity, and intentions live. It anchors many high-frequency idioms: 마음에 들다 (to like / be pleased by something you meet), 마음을 먹다 (to make up one's mind), 마음이 아프다 (to be heartsick). The classic English-speaker pitfall is two-fold: using 마음 for the body-heart (say 심장이 빨리 뛰어요 for a racing heart), and translating 'I like it' as 좋아해요 when you mean a settled approval of something in front of you — Koreans naturally reach for 마음에 들어요 there, where 좋아하다 is a broader 'I like/am fond of.'
마음.explanation: "heart; mind" is 마음 (maeum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 마음이 따뜻해요 ("has a warm heart"). Watch the particle attached to 마음 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
마음.shortExplanation: 마음 means "heart; mind" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 마음 for the physical heart. The organ is 심장 — say 심장이 두근거려요, not 마음이 두근거려요.
Saying 마음에 들어요 about an action you enjoy. 마음에 들다 is for liking a thing/person; for enjoying an activity use 좋아하다 (수영을 좋아해요).
Marking it 마음을 들어요. The fixed idiom is 마음에 들다 with 에 — the thing 'enters into' your heart.

examples.en: That person has a warm heart.
examples.note: Simple: 마음이 + adjective describes someone's inner nature.

examples.en: I really like this gift.
examples.note: Everyday: 마음에 들다 is THE verb for liking things/people you encounter.

examples.en: Feeling sorry, I reached out first.
examples.note: Real situation: 마음에 = 'out of (a feeling),' a common motive marker.

ex.ko: 관용구는 글자 그대로 풀면 뜻이 통하지 않으므로 통째로 외우는 게 좋아요.
ex.en: Idioms don't make sense word by word, so it's best to memorise them whole.
ex.note: -(으)므로 from the written-style chapter, used here in ordinary speech.

ex.ko: 속담은 문장을 새로 만들지 않고 통째로 인용해요.
ex.en: You quote a proverb whole rather than building a new sentence out of it.
ex.note: This is the single most useful rule for using proverbs correctly.

ex.ko: 그 사람은 우리 동네 마당발이라 모르는 가게가 없어요.
ex.en: He's the neighbourhood's great connector — there's no shop he doesn't know.
ex.note: 마당발 is the noun for the person; 발이 넓다 describes the quality.

ex.ko: 외국에 나가 보고 나서야 제가 우물 안 개구리였다는 걸 알았어요.
ex.en: It was only after going abroad that I realised how narrow my world had been.
ex.note: 우물 안 개구리 is said about oneself far more comfortably than about others.

태산.en: a huge mountain (in the proverb 티끌 모아 태산)

ex.ko: 할 일이 태산인데 아직 시작도 못 했어요.
ex.en: I have a mountain of things to do and haven't even started.
ex.note: 할 일이 태산이다 is the other everyday use of 태산.
